Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

fields.abstract: We propose Pseudo Multi-Labels for single-positive multi-label (SPML) learning, a setting where each image has only one confirmed positive label and the remaining labels are unknown. The method trains a teacher network on SPML annotations and then uses the teacher's predictions as pseudo ground-truth labels to train a student network on fully labeled images. This simple self-training approach helps recover missing supervision and improves multi-label classification performance, with the student model approaching the performance of a model trained on fully annotated data.
fields.additional_notes: Submitted as a Tiny Paper at ICLR 2023.
fields.title: Pseudo Labels for Single Positive Multi-Label Learning

fields.abstract: Epistemic voting interprets votes as noisy signals about a ground truth. We study settings where the truth is a set of winning alternatives whose cardinality is known only within lower and upper bounds, as in multi-label annotation with prior knowledge on the number of labels. We propose noise models and aggregation rules that return sets of winners as local maxima of the data likelihood. We also report experiments on multi-label annotations that we collected.

fields.abstract: This paper proposes a safety-critical obstacle avoidance control approach for autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) with disturbances and uncertainties. Existing exponential control barrier functions (ECBFs) are extended to handle unknown disturbances, leading to input-to-state safe exponential control barrier functions (ISSf-ECBFs). An extended state observer is used to estimate unknown external marine disturbances and internal model uncertainties, and an anti-disturbance controller is designed accordingly. Based on the proposed ISSf-ECBFs, a quadratic programming problem is formulated to determine the optimal control input. The closed-loop system is proven to be input-to-state safe and uniformly ultimately bounded. Simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed control strategy.
keywords: input-to-state safe exponential control barrier functions

fields.abstract: 3D perceptual representations are well suited for robot manipulation as they encode occlusions and simplify spatial reasoning. However, many manipulation tasks require high spatial precision in end-effector pose prediction, which often demands expensive high-resolution 3D feature grids. We introduce Act3D, a manipulation policy transformer that represents the robot workspace using a 3D feature field with adaptive resolutions based on the task. The model lifts 2D pre-trained features to 3D using sensed depth, attends to sampled 3D points, and uses coarse-to-fine point sampling with relative-position attention to efficiently compute high-resolution 3D action maps. Act3D achieves state-of-the-art performance on RLBench, improving over prior 2D multi-view and 3D policies while using less compute. Ablations quantify the impact of spatial attention, large-scale vision-language pre-trained backbones, and weight tying across coarse-to-fine attention stages.

fields.abstract: Monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a critical problem in robotics and autonomous driving. Traditional methods solve this problem with filtering or optimization, but they often require manual tuning. Learning-based approaches can be end-to-end, but they typically rely on large models with many parameters and limited interpretability. We propose a fully differentiable and interpretable bird-eye-view (BEV) based VIO model for robots with local planar motion that can be trained without deep neural networks. The method uses an Unscented Kalman Filter as a differentiable layer to estimate pitch and roll while learning the noise covariance matrices, applies differentiable camera projection to generate gravity-aligned BEV images, and then uses a differentiable pose estimator to recover the remaining motion, yielding 5-DoF pose estimation. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the proposed approach is competitive with state-of-the-art methods and generalizes well to unseen scenes.
fields.additional_notes: This work is a strong fit for a robotics-learning venue because it targets visual-inertial odometry for robots and autonomous driving. Consider including a clear limitations section and emphasizing real-world transfer and robotics relevance in the final submission.

source_extraction.abstract: Monocular visual-inertial odometry (VIO) is a critical problem in robotics and autonomous driving. Traditional methods solve this problem based on filtering or optimization. While being fully interpretable, they rely on manual interference and empirical parameter tuning. On the other hand, learning-based approaches allow for end-to-end training but require a large number of training data to learn millions of parameters. However, the non-interpretable and heavy models hinder the generalization ability. In this paper, we propose a fully differentiable, and interpretable, bird-eye-view (BEV) based VIO model for robots with local planar motion that can be trained without deep neural networks. Specifically, we first adopt Unscented Kalman Filter as a differentiable layer to predict the pitch and roll, where the covariance matrices of noise are learned to filter out the noise of the IMU raw data. Second, the refined pitch and roll are adopted to retrieve a gravity-aligned BEV image of each frame using differentiable camera projection. Finally, a differentiable pose estimator is utilized to estimate the remaining 3 DoF poses between the BEV frames: leading to a 5 DoF pose estimation. Our method allows for learning the covariance matrices end-to-end supervised by the pose estimation loss, demonstrating superior performance to empirical baselines. Experimental results on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our simple approach is competitive with state-of-the-art methods and generalizes well on unseen scenes.

fields.abstract: Robotic manipulation can benefit from the data efficiency, robustness, and predictability of model-based methods if robots can quickly generate models of novel objects. This is difficult when complex joint friction lacks clear first-principles models and when numerically stiff contact dynamics make standard model-building approaches struggle. We propose a method to simultaneously learn contact and continuous dynamics of a novel, possibly multi-link object by observing motion through contact-rich trajectories. Our method formulates system identification as a loss that infers unmeasured contact forces while penalizing violations of physical constraints and laws of motion under the current model parameters. Unlike prediction-based losses used in differentiable simulation, the proposed objective learns dynamics more directly. Using a new dataset of real articulated object trajectories and an existing cube toss dataset, the method outperforms differentiable simulation and end-to-end alternatives while using less data.

fields.abstract: Colonoscopy is a key screening tool for colorectal cancer, but automated polyp segmentation methods often struggle with real-time performance and generalization across centers. We propose TransNetR, a transformer-based residual encoder-decoder network for colon polyp segmentation that uses a pre-trained ResNet50 encoder, three decoder blocks, and a final upsampling layer. We further evaluate the model under out-of-distribution conditions on PolypGen and two additional polyp segmentation benchmarks, showing strong generalization across multiple centers and state-of-the-art performance in these tests.

fields.abstract: Link prediction is a core task in graph learning with broad practical applications such as friend recommendation. Recent models commonly use either Dot Product or HadamardMLP decoders to score candidate edges from node embeddings. After theoretical and empirical analysis, we find that HadamardMLP decoders are generally more effective for link prediction, but they lack scalable top-neighbor retrieval on large graphs. To address this, we propose Flashlight, a sublinear algorithm that accelerates top scoring neighbor retrieval for HadamardMLP by progressively applying approximate maximum inner product search with adaptively adjusted query embeddings. Experiments show that Flashlight improves link prediction inference speed by more than 100x on the OGBL-CITATION2 dataset without sacrificing effectiveness, enabling large-scale applications with more effective decoders.

Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

fields.abstract: We study fairness in the context of feature-based price discrimination in monopoly markets. We propose a new notion of individual fairness, namely, alpha-fairness, which guarantees that individuals with similar features face similar prices. First, we study a discrete valuation space and give an analytical solution for optimal fair feature-based pricing. We show that the cost of fair pricing, defined as the ratio of expected revenue under optimal feature-based pricing to that under optimal fair feature-based pricing, can be arbitrarily large in general. When the revenue function is continuous and concave with respect to prices, we show that one can achieve a cost of fairness strictly less than 2, irrespective of the model parameters. Finally, we provide an algorithm to compute a fair feature-based pricing strategy that achieves this cost of fairness.

fields.abstract: Searching for a path between two nodes in a graph is a fundamental problem across domains such as robotics, AI, and biology. We present PHIL (Path Heuristic with Imitation Learning), a neural architecture and training algorithm for discovering graph search and navigation heuristics from data by combining imitation learning with graph representation learning. PHIL trains a specialized graph neural network-based heuristic on search trajectories and shortest-path distances using backpropagation through the path-finding process. The learned heuristic produces graph embeddings useful for inferring node distances, runs in constant time with respect to graph size, and can be integrated with algorithms such as A*. Experiments show that PHIL reduces explored nodes by 58.5% on average over benchmark datasets and transfers across diverse graph domains, including biological networks and road networks.

Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

fields.abstract: Stochastic gradient descent is widely used to optimize deep neural networks, but its gradient estimates can be noisy and unstable, which can slow convergence and hurt performance. We propose Filter Gradient Descent (FGD), a family of stochastic optimization algorithms that estimates the local gradient by solving an adaptive filtering problem over historical gradients. By incorporating past states, FGD reduces gradient variance and improves estimation quality. Experiments on numerical optimization and neural network training show that FGD is more robust than traditional momentum-based methods and can improve optimization performance.

fields.abstract: There is emerging research interest in addressing the online 3D bin packing problem (3D-BPP), which has wide applications in logistics. However, neither heuristic methods nor deep reinforcement learning (DRL) methods outperform human packers in real logistics scenarios. One important reason is that humans can correct inappropriate packing actions by unpacking incorrectly packed items. Inspired by this unpacking mechanism, we present a DRL-based packing-and-unpacking network (PUN) to learn the synergies between these two actions for online 3D-BPP. Experimental results show that PUN achieves state-of-the-art performance, and the supplementary video demonstrates that the system can reliably complete the online 3D bin packing task in the real world.

fields.abstract: A robot operating in a partially observable environment must perform sensing actions to achieve a goal, such as clearing objects in front of a shelf to better localize a target object and estimate its shape for grasping. A POMDP is a principled framework for enabling robots to perform such information-gathering actions. However, while robot manipulation domains involve high-dimensional and continuous observation and action spaces, most POMDP solvers are limited to discrete spaces. Recent work on POMCPOW extends online planning to continuous POMDPs using sampling and progressive widening, but it remains too slow for manipulation problems with camera observations and multiple objects. We propose a framework that learns to guide POMCPOW from past planning experience using preference learning over success and failure trajectories, with preference labels derived from tree-search results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in several continuous partially observable robotics domains, including real-world manipulation, where the method explicitly reasons about uncertainty in off-the-shelf segmentation and pose estimation algorithms.

fields.abstract: We propose a bootstrap-based online algorithm for stochastic linear bandit problems. The method, LinReBoot, uses residual bootstrap exploration to estimate the next-step reward by resampling residuals from the mean reward estimate and selecting the arm with the highest estimated reward. We develop a theoretical framework to explain residual-bootstrap exploration in stochastic linear bandits and show that the resulting optimistic behavior yields a high-probability sublinear regret bound under mild conditions. Experiments demonstrate that LinReBoot is computationally efficient, generalizes well across linear bandit formulations, and performs competitively with existing methods such as Linear Thompson Sampling, Linear PHE, Linear GIRO, and Linear UCB.

fields.abstract: Robots in complex multi-agent environments must reason about observed and unobserved agents under partial observability. We present Active Visual Planning (AVP), a learning-based method for prediction and planning that uses high-dimensional observations to learn a flow-based generative model of multi-agent joint trajectories, including agents that may be revealed in the future depending on the robot's actions. The model is trained offline from recorded observations rather than ground-truth states and supports contingency planning over the possible existence, intentions, and positions of unobserved agents. We demonstrate AVP in autonomous driving environments inspired by real-world scenarios, where it achieves expert-level closed-loop performance and outperforms methods that do not explicitly reason about unobserved agents.

fields.abstract: We propose a disentangled latent diffusion model (DLDM) for generating multi-modal brain tumor MRI without requiring a source image. The method first trains an autoencoder to separate modality-sharing structural information from modality-specific style information in the latent space, then uses a diffusion model to synthesize these latent codes. By fixing structure and varying style, DLDM can generate diverse multi-modal MR images while preserving consistent brain anatomy. We evaluate the approach with clean-FID and improved precision and recall, and compare it against GAN-based baselines such as StyleGAN2.

Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

fields.abstract: Dynamic network flow models have been extensively studied and widely used to formulate real-world control problems such as transportation, supply chain management, and power grid control. However, existing time-expansion and optimization-based methods struggle to scale to large dynamic networks and are limited in handling stochastic, nonlinear, or unknown dynamics. fields.abstract: We study top-K recovery from passively collected discrete choice data, where each observation consists of a user selecting one item from a menu. To address this problem, we propose the choice-based Borda count algorithm, a fast and accurate ranking method for identifying the top K items from a large pool. source_extraction.abstract: The intersection of learning to rank and choice modeling is an active area of research with applications in e-commerce, information retrieval and the social sciences. In some applications such as recommendation systems, the statistician is primarily interested in recovering the set of the top ranked items from a large pool of items as efficiently as possible using passively collected \emph{discrete choice data}, i.e., the user picks one item from a set of multiple items. Motivated by this practical consideration, we propose \emph{the choice-based Borda count algorithm} as a fast and accurate ranking algorithm for \emph{top $K$-recovery} i.e., correctly identifying all of the top $K$ items. We show that the choice-based Borda count algorithm has optimal sample complexity for top-$K$ recovery under a broad class of \emph{random utility models}. We prove that in the limit, the choice-based Borda count algorithm produces the same top-$K$ estimate as the commonly used Maximum Likelihood Estimate method but the former's speed and simplicity brings considerable advantages in practice. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets show that the counting algorithm is competitive with commonly used ranking algorithms in terms of accuracy while being several orders of magnitude faster.

fields.abstract: This paper explores training medical vision-language models (VLMs), where visual and language inputs are embedded into a common space, with a particular focus on scenarios where training data is limited, as is often the case in clinical datasets. We explore several candidate methods to improve low-data performance, including: (i) adapting generic pre-trained models to novel image and text domains; (ii) using local and global contrastive loss functions, as well as combinations of the two; and (iii) adding extra supervision during VLM training through image- and text-only self-supervision and by creating additional positive image-text pairs through augmentation and nearest-neighbour search. Using text-to-image retrieval as a benchmark, we evaluate these methods with variable-sized training datasets of paired chest X-rays and radiological reports. Combined, they significantly improve retrieval compared with fine-tuning CLIP, roughly equivalent to training with 10x the data. Similar gains are found in downstream classification of CXR-related conditions, where our method outperforms CLIP and BioVIL in zero-shot and linear-probing settings. We conclude with recommendations for researchers training vision-language models on other medical imaging modalities when training data is scarce, and we release our code to support further research.

fields.abstract: Existing imitation learning work usually assumes that the demonstrator and imitator share the same dynamics, which limits the use of demonstrations collected from other agents or robots. We study out-of-dynamics imitation learning (OOD-IL), where the demonstrator and imitator share the same state space but may differ in action space and dynamics. source_extraction.abstract: Existing imitation learning works mainly assume that the demonstrator who collects demonstrations shares the same dynamics as the imitator. However, the assumption limits the usage of imitation learning, especially when collecting demonstrations for the imitator is difficult. In this paper, we study out-of-dynamics imitation learning (OOD-IL), which relaxes the assumption to that the demonstrator and the imitator have the same state spaces but could have different action spaces and dynamics. OOD-IL enables imitation learning to utilize demonstrations from a wide range of demonstrators but introduces a new challenge: some demonstrations cannot be achieved by the imitator due to the different dynamics. Prior works try to filter out such demonstrations by feasibility measurements, but ignore the fact that the demonstrations exhibit a multimodal distribution since the different demonstrators may take different policies in different dynamics. We develop a better transferability measurement to tackle this newly-emerged challenge. We firstly design a novel sequence-based contrastive clustering algorithm to cluster demonstrations from the same mode to avoid the mutual interference of demonstrations from different modes, and then learn the transferability of each demonstration with an adversarial-learning based algorithm in each cluster. Experiment results on several MuJoCo environments, a driving environment, and a simulated robot environment show that the proposed transferability measurement more accurately finds and down-weights non-transferable demonstrations and outperforms prior works on the final imitation learning performance. We show the videos of our experiment results on our website.

Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

source_extraction.abstract: Contact is at the core of robotic manipulation. At times, it is desired (e.g. manipulation and grasping), and at times, it is harmful (e.g. when avoiding obstacles). However, traditional path planning algorithms focus solely on collision-free paths, limiting their applicability in contact-rich tasks. To address this limitation, we propose the domain of Language-Conditioned Path Planning, where contact-awareness is incorporated into the path planning problem. As a first step in this domain, we propose Language-Conditioned Collision Functions (LACO), a novel approach that learns a collision function using only a single-view image, language prompt, and robot configuration. fields.abstract: The cornerstone of neural algorithmic reasoning is the ability to solve algorithmic tasks that generalise out of distribution. While recent work has improved this area, it has largely focused on specialist models. Here we instead develop a generalist neural algorithmic learner: a single graph neural network processor that can learn to execute a wide range of algorithms, including sorting, searching, dynamic programming, path-finding, and geometry. Using the CLRS benchmark, we show that generalist algorithmic learners can be built by incorporating knowledge from specialist models. We present improvements to the input representation, training regime, and processor architecture that raise average single-task performance by more than 20% over prior work, and we study multi-task learning with these improvements. The results demonstrate a generalist learner that effectively transfers knowledge captured by specialist models.

source_extraction.abstract: The cornerstone of neural algorithmic reasoning is the ability to solve algorithmic tasks, especially in a way that generalises out of distribution. While recent years have seen a surge in methodological improvements in this area, they mostly focused on building specialist models. Specialist models are capable of learning to neurally execute either only one algorithm or a collection of algorithms with identical control-flow backbone. Here, instead, we focus on constructing a generalist neural algorithmic learner---a single graph neural network processor capable of learning to execute a wide range of algorithms, such as sorting, searching, dynamic programming, path-finding and geometry. We leverage the CLRS benchmark to empirically show that, much like recent successes in the domain of perception, generalist algorithmic learners can be built by "incorporating" knowledge. That is, it is possible to effectively learn algorithms in a multi-task manner, so long as we can learn to execute them well in a single-task regime. Motivated by this, we present a series of improvements to the input representation, training regime and processor architecture over CLRS, improving average single-task performance by over 20% from prior art. We then conduct a thorough ablation of multi-task learners leveraging these improvements. Call for Tiny Papers, a DEI initiative

Email: iclr.dei.2023@gmail.com

Accepted conference papers at ICLR represent a high level of scientific quality. The other side of the coin is that they can be out of reach for those starting out, or from different backgrounds. We want paper publishing to be not only a showcase of achievements, but also a marker for valuable learning experiences made accessible to beginners and outsiders. Devising more ways to mark milestones and measure growth in an individual, or community’s maturity, is greatly conducive to both continually pushing the frontiers of science, and lifting people up in this process.

Researchers from underrepresented backgrounds are not necessarily equipped with the same resources to publish full papers from the start of their scientific journeys. To create a more inclusive ICLR community, we as organizers need to create more pathways, and reasons for people from various backgrounds to enter, stay, and grow in the machine learning community.

To that end, we are launching a more approachable format to publish, kick-start, and collaborate on ideas, “Tiny Papers,” as part of the DEI initiative of ICLR 2023, with the hope to attract more underrepresented, under-resourced, and budding researchers to join the community in a meaningful way. Not only will this additional, and different, venue to publish usher in new researchers, it will also serve as an efficient platform for disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

The objective of the new “Tiny Papers” track at ICLR is threefold:
1. Creating alternative, complementary, and diverse entry points to research. And in particular, creating approachable avenues for beginners to enter and enjoy the ICLR community.
2. Celebrating intermediate breakthroughs in machine learning.
3. Efficiently disseminating ideas, findings, and opinions.

As the Tiny Papers track is a Diveristy, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) initiative, orgnized by the DEI Chairs of ICLR 2023, we require every submission to have at least one key author that meets the underrepresented minority (URM) criteria.

Despite the wide range of topics that could benefit from the Tiny Papers format, we focus the type of submissions to be the following:
- An implementation and experimentation of a novel (not published elsewhere) yet simple idea, or a modest and self-contained theoretical result
- A follow-up experiment to or re-analysis of a previously published paper
- A new perspective on a previously published paper

Key Dates
Submission portal opens: February 1st, 2023
Submission deadline: February 28th, 2023 AoE
Notification of acceptance: April 10th, 2023
Tiny Papers Showcase Day: May 5th, 2023
Camera-ready deadline (for archival): May 31st, 2023

Submission Guidelines

Underrepresented minority (URM) criteria
Each Tiny Paper needs its first or last author to qualify as an underrepresented minority (URM). Authors don't have to reveal how they qualify, and may just self-identify that they qualify.

Submissions have to include a "URM Statement" section which acklnowledges meeting the URM criteria. See the corresponding section in our provided LaTex teamplate for examples. The URM Statement section does not count into the page limit.

Formatting and author guidelines
The guidelines and restrictions for this Tiny Papers track are:
- Write a paper with the same structure as seen in full papers, but with at most 2 pages of main text. References, Appendices, and URM Stement sections do not count towards the page limit, but we do not recommend dissecting a regular length paper into a tiny paper by moving the majority of the content into appendices.
- It is recommended to have 1-2 figures, 1 table, and 4-5 sections. But authors are free to use their own structure.
- The submission portal, hosted at OpenReivew, opens Feb 1st, 2023. Please check back on this page, or watch @iclr_conf on Twitter.

All Tiny Papers should comply with the conference paper formatting requirements. We provide a slightly edited LaTeX template for authors to use. Authors should submit their Tiny Paper with the authors names and affiliations anonymised, as in the conference paper track.

Reviewing Instructions
Tiny Papers should be clear, correct, and reproducible. It is not necessary that submissions be “significant”, “impactful”, “novel”, or reach a new state-of-the-art on benchmarks. In this way, our reviewing philosophy is inspired by venues like eLife and TMLR.

fields.abstract: We introduce PRISM, a method for real-time filtering in a probabilistic generative model of agent motion and visual perception. Previous approaches either lack uncertainty estimates for the map and agent state, do not run in real-time, do not have a dense scene representation, or do not model agent dynamics. Our solution reconciles all of these aspects. We start from a predefined state-space model that combines differentiable rendering and 6-DoF dynamics. Probabilistic inference in this model amounts to simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM) and is intractable. We use a series of approximations to Bayesian inference to arrive at probabilistic map and state estimates. We take advantage of well-established methods and closed-form updates, preserving accuracy and enabling real-time capability. The proposed solution runs at 10Hz real-time and is similarly accurate to state-of-the-art SLAM in small to medium-sized indoor environments, with high-speed UAV and handheld camera agents (Blackbird, EuRoC, and TUM-RGBD).

fields.abstract: Recent advances in computer vision often rely on large models trained on vast amounts of labeled or unlabeled data, which can be difficult to use in resource-constrained settings. We present Astroformer, a hybrid transformer-convolutional architecture for galaxy morphology classification that is designed to work well in low-data regimes. The model combines a new network stack design, a modified relative self-attention mechanism, and carefully chosen data augmentation and regularization. On the Galaxy10 DECals dataset, Astroformer achieves 94.86% top-1 accuracy and sets a new state of the art, and it also improves results on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. Our experiments suggest that methods tuned for large datasets do not necessarily transfer well when data is limited.

Furthermore, this approach also sets a new state-of-the-art on CIFAR-100 and Tiny ImageNet. We also find that models and training methods used for larger datasets would often not work very well in the low-data regime. fields.abstract: We propose SCALE, an approach for discovering and learning a diverse set of interpretable robot skills from a limited dataset. Rather than learning a single skill that may miss important modes in the data, we identify different modes through causal reasoning and learn a separate skill for each one. SCALE associates each mode with a set of causally relevant context variables discovered by causal interventions in simulation, enabling data partitioning by causal process and training compressed skills that ignore irrelevant variables. We model each robot skill as a Regional Compressed Option linked to a local causal process and its relevant variables. We demonstrate the approach on block stacking and peg-in-hole insertion under uncertainty, and show that the learned skills are compact, robust to domain shift, and suitable for sim-to-real transfer.

source_extraction.abstract: We propose SCALE, an approach for discovering and learning a diverse set of interpretable robot skills from a limited dataset. Rather than learning a single skill which may fail to capture all the modes in the data, we first identify the different modes via causal reasoning and learn a separate skill for each of them. Our main insight is to associate each mode with a unique set of causally relevant context variables that are discovered by performing causal interventions in simulation. This enables data partitioning based on the causal processes that generated the data, and then compressed skills that ignore the irrelevant variables can be trained. We model each robot skill as a Regional Compressed Option, which extends the options framework by associating a causal process and its relevant variables with the option. Modeled as the skill Data Generating Region, each causal process is local in nature and hence valid over only a subset of the context space. We demonstrate our approach for two representative manipulation tasks: block stacking and peg-in-hole insertion under uncertainty. Our experiments show that our approach yields diverse skills that are compact, robust to domain shifts, and suitable for sim-to-real transfer.

fields.abstract: We present a seeing-eye quadruped navigation system that is robust to external human tugging forces and can estimate the direction and magnitude of those forces during blindfolded co-navigation. The method jointly trains a locomotion controller with reinforcement learning to remain stable under perturbations and a force estimator with supervised learning using onboard sensors only. At deployment, the estimator detects human tugs from joint encoders and IMU measurements, and the resulting force estimates inform global navigation decisions while a local planner handles obstacle avoidance using LIDAR. We evaluate the system in simulation and on a real quadruped robot, showing robust locomotion under external forces, accurate force-direction detection, and a full hardware demonstration with a blindfolded human.

source_extraction.abstract: Seeing-eye robots are very useful tools for guiding visually impaired people, potentially producing a huge societal impact given the low availability and high cost of real guide dogs. Although a few seeing-eye robot systems have already been demonstrated, none considered external tugs from humans, which frequently occur in a real guide dog setting. In this paper, we simultaneously train a locomotion controller that is robust to external tugging forces via Reinforcement Learning~(RL), and an external force estimator via supervised learning. The controller ensures stable walking, and the force estimator enables the robot to respond to the external forces from the human. These forces are used to guide the robot to the global goal, which is unknown to the robot, while the robot guides the human around nearby obstacles via a local planner. Experimental results in simulation and on hardware show that our controller is robust to external forces, and our seeing-eye system can accurately detect force direction. We demonstrate our full seeing-eye robot system on a real quadruped robot with a blindfolded human.
